title: With Due Respect (Vol. 2) -- Ch. 5: Chief Justice of the Philippines
keywords: Special Allowance for the Judiciary Law
primary_topics: Chapter 5 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 2) -- CJP's December 27, 2009 Inquirer column cataloguing the eight functions of the Chief Justice, written as the country looked to the Court amid abuses by elected officials

The CJ as 'primus inter pares' (first among equals) who presides over and shapes the Court's work but holds only one vote, ruling by 'moral ascendancy and persuasive skill,' not a boss-subordinate relationship

The CJ as chief executive of the whole judiciary (2,000 judges, 26,000 employees), passionate reformer, leader of the bar, academic 'maestro' (PHILJA chair), JBC 'mover and shaker,' and administrator/financial steward of the judicial budget (JDF and SAJ)

The CJ as role model and exemplar -- leading 'the last bulwark of democracy' while attending to many sensitive, non-judicial leadership duties, so that he is 'more accurately addressed' as Chief Justice of the Philippines, not just of the Supreme Court
sub_topics: Why the people turn to the CJ: in turmoil they should look to elected leaders, but since the 'abusive and illegal acts' often come from executive officials, they turn to the CJ to lead the Court in protecting their rights

Function 1 -- primus inter pares: the CJ presides over sessions, controls the flow, shapes the agenda, and influences the Court's direction, yet has 'only one vote,' relying on moral ascendancy and persuasion
Function 2 -- leader of the entire judiciary: the CEO of 2,000 lower-court judges and 26,000 employees, who must both honor precedent (the jurist) and 'innovate, re-engineer' (the leader)

Function 3 -- passionate reformer and action person: driving speedy, equal justice and automation in the Information Age, interacting with agencies and even foreign institutions in a 'sensitive balancing act' that demands public trust in his integrity and independence
Function 4 -- leader of the bar: with the Court's supervision over the practice of law, all lawyers and bar associations look to the CJ for guidance

Function 5 -- academic and maestro: as ex-officio chair of the Philippine Judicial Academy, the CJ is a 'guru' for the continuing education of judges, often turning to outside assistance for lack of resources

Function 6 -- mover and shaker: as JBC chair, finding better ways to search, screen and select judges -- 'the need for quality judgments begins with quality judges' -- and working for better pay, security and facilities to attract the best lawyers

Function 7 -- administrator, manager, and financial wizard: under the Constitution's 'administrative supervision over all courts,' plus the Administrative Code, the GAA, the Judiciary Development Fund Law (PD 1949) and the SAJ Law (RA 9227), which give the CJ 'exclusive sole power' to disburse the JDF and SAJ funds

Function 8 -- role model and exemplar of public service: under the 'minute scrutiny' of an inquisitive media, the CJ is the people's choice of an upright public servant, sought by civic groups for his 'quiet persona' in times of political wrangling

stances.claim: Because the CJ leads the judiciary as 'the last bulwark of democracy' and carries leadership duties to 'the farthest corners of the country,' he is 'more accurately addressed' as Chief Justice of the Philippines, not merely of the Supreme Court.

notable_anecdotes: Only one vote: CJP underscores that for all his agenda-shaping power, the CJ casts 'only one vote' and must sway colleagues by persuasion, not command.

Quality judges first: he distills the JBC mission to a maxim -- 'the need for quality judgments begins with quality judges' -- justifying his push for better pay and facilities to attract the best lawyers.
'Exclusive sole power' over the funds: he notes that the JDF Law (PD 1949) and SAJ Law (RA 9227) place the disbursement of those judiciary funds in the CJ's hands, making him a 'financial wizard.'
The quiet persona: he observes that civic and non-partisan groups, in times of political wrangling, 'find solace and peace' in the CJ's quiet bearing and seek him to grace their inductions.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 5 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 2), CJP's December 27, 2009 Inquirer column, catalogues the eight functions of the Chief Justice, written as a turmoil-weary public looked to the Court -- for though they should turn to elected leaders, the abuses they complain of 'come mainly from executive officials.' First, the CJ is 'primus inter pares,' presiding over and shaping the Court's work yet holding 'only one vote,' so he leads by 'moral ascendancy and persuasive skill, not a boss-subordinate relationship.' Second, he is the chief executive of the entire judiciary -- 2,000 judges and 26,000 employees -- who must both honor precedent and 'innovate, re-engineer' the branch. Third, he is a passionate reformer driving speedy justice and automation, interacting even with foreign institutions in a 'sensitive balancing act' that demands public trust in his integrity and independence. Fourth, as the Court supervises the practice of law, he is leader of the bar; fifth, as ex-officio chair of the Philippine Judicial Academy, he is the academic 'maestro' of judicial education; sixth, as JBC chair he is the 'mover and shaker' of judicial selection, since 'the need for quality judgments begins with quality judges'; and seventh, he is the 'administrator, manager, and financial wizard' who, under the Constitution, the Administrative Code, the GAA, the JDF Law (PD 1949) and the SAJ Law (RA 9227), wields 'exclusive sole power' to disburse the judiciary's funds. Eighth, under the 'minute scrutiny' of an inquisitive media, he is a role model and exemplar of public service whose 'quiet persona' draws civic groups in times of political wrangling. In sum, leading 'the last bulwark of democracy' while carrying leadership duties 'to the farthest corners of the country,' the CJ is, CJP argues, 'more accurately addressed' as Chief Justice of the Philippines, not just of the Supreme Court.
